It is a genuine pre-read reject signal in the sense the question asks — it costs one `wc` and no source fetch — but only over a set. A 25-section block at 1.7/1k against a corpus at 7.5/1k is a read-order instruction, not a verdict.

findings.claim: In badresearch's funnel, popularity beats every quality dimension COMBINED by design, and the arithmetic is exact. The composite is `rrf + utility/18 * (1/60)`. The full 0->18 utility swing is worth 1/60 = 0.01667. One extra SERP sighting at rank 1 is worth 1/(60+1) = 0.01639. So a candidate that appears in two more (query, provider) lists outranks a candidate with a perfect authority+novelty+stance+coverage+redundancy+freshness score. RRF consensus is explicitly uncapped.
findings.evidence: /Users/seventyleven/Desktop/badresearch/src/bad_research/funnel/rank.py:131 `return rrf + util * (1.0 / rrf_k)`; :48 'Consensus is deliberately UNCAPPED: appearing in every list of a 100-query plan is the strongest un-read relevance evidence the funnel can observe'; :85 `novelty = 3 if n_prov == 1 else (1 if n_prov == 2 else 0)`. Arithmetic computed live.
findings.accretes: No. Fixed k=60, fixed 6x3 rubric, hardcoded `_PRIMARY`/`_INSTITUTIONAL`/`_BLOG` substring tuples. The rank order for a given SERP set is identical on run 1 and run 1,000.
findings.false_negative_cost: The inversion is inside the scorer and fights itself: the RRF term rewards many-provider consensus without bound while the novelty dimension rewards single-provider obscurity (n_prov==1 -> 3). The anti-popularity correction maxes at 3/18 * 1/60 = 0.00278, which is **5.9x weaker** than one extra rank-1 sighting. A source only one provider ever surfaced — the definition of the obscure tail — is structurally outranked. Nothing measures what this loses; there is no held-out set of known-good obscure sources anywhere in the funnel or its tests.
findings.what_it_would_change: Either cap the RRF consensus term (the docstring argues against this on purpose, citing issue #40) or move novelty out of the 1/60-scaled utility and into its own additive term at RRF magnitude. Whichever is chosen, the decision needs a held-out set of sources known to be good and known to be rare, because right now the tradeoff is being made by a scale factor nobody has tested against an outcome.

findings.claim: The one instrument on disk that computes a FALSE-NEGATIVE number is checks/coverage.py — Lincoln-Petersen capture-recapture over two independent search passes — and it is the only place that encodes exactly where popularity inverts: two rank-ordered passes agree about the head and are silent about the tail TOGETHER, so their inflated overlap shrinks the estimated population and reports HIGH coverage precisely when the obscure tail was missed by both. It refuses to produce an estimate rather than produce a flattering one.

findings.accretes: Yes, in the only sense that holds up: the estimate genuinely sharpens as passes accumulate — two lanes give one pair, three give three pairs and a worst-case bound, and the singleton fraction falls as the tail is actually reached. That is the right failure, and it means a run whose only two lanes are both popularity-ranked gets no coverage number at all — which will be the common case for anyone searching the live web with two SERP providers. Its sibling discipline appears in figure_support.py, which counts `unchecked` separately from `checked` with the comment 'a prose claim: counted, never called clean'.
findings.what_it_would_change: This is the mechanism to generalise, and it applies directly to the transcript corpus: run two genuinely different extraction passes over one source (e.g. entity extraction vs. figure extraction, or note-side vs. source-side) and read the singleton fraction as the shape of what a single pass misses. findings.claim: The exchange rate for a second independent reader is measured and near-symmetric: one screener gets sensitivity 86.6% (95% CI 80.6–91.2) / specificity 79.2%; two screeners OR-combined get 97.5% (95.1–98.8) / 68.7%. Buying +10.9pp of recall costs −10.5pp of specificity — redundancy is not free, it is a trade the field makes knowingly because the loss function is asymmetric.
findings.evidence: Gartlehner et al. 2020, J Clin Epidemiol, DOI 10.1016/j.jclinepi.2020.01.005 — crowd-based parallel-group RCT, 280 participants, 24,942 screening decisions on 2,000 abstracts, each abstract screened ~12 times, two published SRs as reference standards. Abstract retrieved verbatim from Europe PMC search API (resultType=core).
findings.accretes: No — this is a fixed structural choice (n readers), not a learned filter. But it sets the ceiling the accreting mechanisms in findings 4 and 5 are measured against: 97.5% is what two humans achieve, and the Cochrane classifier (finding 2) is justified explicitly by beating that class of incumbent.
findings.false_negative_cost: Directly measured as the 13.4% of relevant abstracts a single reader loses. Nobody in this dataset measures what those specific 13.4% were worth — see finding 6, where only one paper in the lane goes downstream to 'did the answer change'.
findings.what_it_would_change: The funnel currently has one reader per candidate. If a second independent pass is added, budget for the specificity loss up front: at these ratios a 2-of-2 AND-rule would restore precision but reintroduce the single-reader recall, and an OR-rule roughly doubles the read cost of Stage E. The number to steal is the ratio, not the design: 1pp of recall costs ~1pp of specificity in this regime.

findings.claim: The shipped Cochrane RCT Classifier rejects candidates before any full-text read using a three-dataset procedure with a hard abstain rule: train (280,620 Embase records, 20,454 = 7.3% positive), calibrate the threshold on a DIFFERENT set (49,025 Clinical Hedges records) by ordering all records by score and reading off the probability at exactly 99% recall, then evaluate recall on a THIRD set of 58,283 studies actually included in 4,296 real Cochrane Reviews. At the chosen threshold: precision 8.3% (1 in 12 retrieved is a true positive), specificity 0.63, C=0.978, Brier 0.048, and 58% of records auto-discarded.
findings.evidence: Thomas et al. 2021, J Clin Epidemiol 133:140-151, PMC8168828 §3.1–3.2 and Table 2/Table 3. Local copy: scratchpad/pmc/PMC8168828.txt.
findings.accretes: Partly. The threshold is fit once against a labelled calibration corpus and frozen; it does not move as a review proceeds. What accretes is the label corpus itself — Cochrane Crowd keeps labelling, and the classifier is retrained. The per-run accretion is absent by design here, and finding 4 is the mechanism that supplies it.
findings.false_negative_cost: Measured on real inclusions, not on held-out labels: 224 of 44,007 RCTs lost (0.5%). Losses are time-skewed — older publications are much more likely to be lost (Fig. 5, RCTs lost per 1,000 published by year), because the filter's discrimination rests on abstract conventions (CONSORT) that did not exist earlier. The blind spot is a function of when the record was written, not of its merit.
findings.what_it_would_change: Adopt the three-set split verbatim for any funnel scoring model: never set a cutoff on the data you fit on, and never validate on labels — validate on the candidates that actually survived to be cited in a finished report. Set the cutoff by walking the score-ordered list to a chosen recall, not by maximising F1.

findings.claim: That classifier's 5.7 points of recall come entirely from an ABSTAIN rule, not from the model: records with fewer than 400 characters of abstract or 15 characters of title are never scored — they route to a human. With thin records fed in, recall is 93.8% (3,600 of 58,283 lost); with them routed out, 99.5% (224 lost). The paper calls 94% 'unacceptably low'.
findings.evidence: Thomas et al. 2021, PMC8168828 §2.6 ('pragmatic cutoffs … 400 characters as a minimum abstract length and 15 characters as a minimum title length') and §3.2 Table 3 + §4.1. Production effect: in calendar 2018 the pipeline spared Cochrane Crowd 185,039 of 449,480 records (41.2%).
findings.accretes: No — a fixed character constant. It is the null-result shape, and it is still the highest-leverage single rule in the whole pipeline. Worth stating plainly: the biggest recall win in a shipped ML screener is a length threshold, not the model.
findings.false_negative_cost: This IS the false-negative control. Without it the pipeline silently deletes 3,600 real included studies; with it, 224. The 3,376-study difference is the measured cost of letting a classifier judge input it cannot see.
findings.what_it_would_change: This is the exact inversion of what badresearch does today. src/bad_research/web/base.py:60 defaults `looks_like_junk(min_chars=300)` and line 76 returns 'Empty or near-empty content' — a DROP. src/bad_research/funnel/filter.py:71-75 is a pure binary keep/drop with no third branch. Cochrane escalates the same class this code deletes. Add an ABSTAIN verdict to looks_like_junk so short-but-real bodies route to a paid read instead of the bin; the prefetched-body carve-out at filter.py:58 (min_chars=1) already proves the floor is wrong for content nobody fetched, it just fixes it for one lane.

findings.claim: The accreting stopping rule that works is a hypergeometric test on the UNSEEN pool: sample from the not-yet-screened remainder, test H0 'recall < target', stop when you can reject it at your chosen confidence. Ranked quasi-sampling saved a mean 17% of work and missed the 95% recall target in 0.95% of cases; random sampling 15% / 3.29%. The cheap heuristics fail: baseline-inclusion-rate sampling missed the target 39.67% of the time with a modal work saving of 0%, and 'stop after 50 consecutive irrelevant' saved 41% of the work but missed the target in 39% of cases.
findings.evidence: Callaghan & Müller-Hansen 2020, Syst Rev 9:273, PMC7700715 §Results, Figs. 5–8. Local copy: scratchpad/pmc/PMC7700715.txt.
findings.accretes: Yes — this is the strongest accretion mechanism in the lane. The criterion is recomputed every iteration from everything screened so far, and its power grows as the seen set grows. Its key property: it is independent of the model. A bad ranker costs work savings and never costs recall, because the guarantee comes from the sample of the remainder, not from the ranker's scores.
findings.false_negative_cost: Bounded by construction and reportable as a sentence: 'we reject the null that recall < 95% at α=0.05'. The paper also names the inversion that kills naive rules — when the ranker is GOOD, a low relevant-rate among unseen documents indicates LOWER recall, not higher, because recall depends on the count of unseen relevant items, not their rate. Two scenarios with an identical 2% relevant rate in the unseen pool have very different recall.
findings.what_it_would_change: The funnel reads top-N by RRF score and stops. Replace 'stop at N' with 'stop when a hypergeometric test on a random sample of the un-read remainder rejects recall < target'. This needs no model change and no new signal — only that a small random slice of the discarded pool gets read. Budget it: on these datasets the guarantee costs about half the work saving a naive heuristic would claim (17% vs 41%), and buys the 39% failure rate down to 0.95%.

findings.claim: The second accreting mechanism is a per-run calibration sample with a kill switch: humans dual-screen ~19% of records to consensus, the automatic filter's rules are then fit against THAT consensus, and if the fitted filter cannot clear Krippendorff's alpha ≥ 0.8 and F1 ≥ 0.9 on the calibration sample, automation is abandoned for that run rather than tuned further. Crucially, if the HUMANS disagree with each other below 0.8 first, the fix is to rewrite the inclusion criteria, not to re-read (Step 2b).
findings.evidence: Syst Rev 2026, PMC13263951, Figs. 1–2 and Steps 2–6. Case example: 2,514 records total; 471 (18.7%) human-consensus calibration sample; 22 prompt iterations to reach F1 0.85 / α 0.83 at low-two-digit-dollar API cost; frozen prompt then run on three model families (GPT-4.0, Claude 3 Sonnet, Gemini Pro 1.0); 1,647 of 2,043 remaining records (81%) got full agreement and were auto-decided; the 396 discordant went to humans; ~$100 in tokens. The kill switch is demonstrated retrospectively on the Meijboom 2021 dataset, where both metrics fell short and the run would have been discontinued at Step 4.
findings.accretes: Yes, and in the way the owner's thesis predicts: the filter's rules are fit to labelled evidence from THIS question, and the fitting is scored against a human gold standard drawn from the same corpus. It also accretes upstream — disagreement is read as evidence the CRITERIA are wrong, so the run's definition of relevance sharpens before any filtering happens.
findings.false_negative_cost: The kill switch is the false-negative control: it costs a few hours and a calibration sample to discover the filter is unsafe for this topic, versus silently deleting. A separate, unmeasured cost surfaced here: Gemini Pro 1.0 REFUSED to classify 15 records containing 'incest', 'pedophilia', 'child trafficking'. That is a systematic, topic-correlated false negative from a safety filter — the model deletes exactly the abuse-research literature, and no accuracy metric detects it because the records never get a label.
findings.what_it_would_change: Add a Stage-0 calibration pass to the funnel: hand-label ~15-20% of candidates before the filter runs, tune the filter against them, and refuse to run the automatic path if it misses a threshold. Concretely, the model-refusal failure needs its own counter — any candidate that comes back with no verdict must be counted and escalated, never silently treated as a reject.

findings.claim: Almost nobody measures what a false negative COSTS. Across 16 full-text screening-methodology papers I read, exactly one goes downstream from 'we missed X%' to 'did the answer change'. Waffenschmidt 2019 found that in 3 of 7 single screenings (18,148 references) the meta-analysis findings would have changed substantially — and all 3 were the same less-experienced reviewer. The other 4, by experienced reviewers, had no or negligible impact. The miss rate itself splits the same way: median 3% missed (range 0–21%) for 6 experienced reviewers vs 13% (0–58%) for 3 inexperienced.
findings.evidence: Waffenschmidt et al. 2019, BMC Med Res Methodol 19:132, PMC6599339, Abstract + Results. Grep run over all 16 local full texts: `grep -c -i -E "change[d]? the (conclusion|finding|result)|impact on the (findings|conclusion|results)|altered the (conclusion|effect estimate)" pmc/*.txt` → 1 non-zero file (PMC6599339), 15 zeros.
findings.accretes: No, and that is the gap. Consequence is measured retrospectively on finished reviews, never fed back into the screening rule. Nothing in this literature makes the filter learn 'this class of miss was expensive'.
findings.false_negative_cost: Bimodal, not proportional. Cost concentrates in a single bad screener rather than spreading across a miss rate — which means an average recall figure hides the whole problem. A corroborating case: a 3-layer GPT-4 screen with overall sensitivity 0.806 nonetheless included ALL 6 and ALL 9 records that actually reached the two meta-analyses (Reg Anesth-adjacent JMIR study, PMC11364944). Recall and consequence-weighted recall diverge sharply, and only the latter is the thing you care about.
findings.what_it_would_change: Instrument the funnel with two different recall numbers, not one: (a) share of relevant candidates retained, and (b) share of candidates that ended up load-bearing in the finished report that the filter would have killed. Metric (b) is cheap once reports exist — every citation in a shipped badresearch report is a labelled positive, and re-running the filter over the discarded pool for those runs is a free retrospective.

findings.claim: The field's standard instrument for measuring screening error is structurally blind to the error class it most cares about. The largest such study — 139,467 citations, 329,332 decisions, 85 reviewers, 25 systematic reviews — reports a 10.76% (95% CI 7.43–14.09) abstract-screening error rate, and then states: 'When both reviewers agree on excluding an abstract, this abstract disappears from the process; thus, a dual erroneous exclusion cannot be assessed.' The concordant false negative is unobservable by construction.
findings.evidence: Wang, Nayfeh, Tetzlaff, O'Blenis, Murad 2020, PLoS One 15(1):e0227742, PMC6959565, Results + Limitations. Funnel shape from the same paper: 18.07% (12.65–23.48) of searched citations pass abstract screening, 5.48% (2.38–8.58) survive full text. Error rate is topic-dependent, 5.76% (hematology) to 21.11% (primary care).
findings.accretes: No. It is a one-off audit. Its real contribution is epistemic: it establishes that the human gold standard used to validate every automated screener is itself ~10.76% wrong, so an automated filter that matches human error is adequate, not deficient.
findings.false_negative_cost: The published 10.76% is a lower bound that specifically excludes the worst case. Any filter validated against 'what two humans agreed to drop' inherits a blind spot of unknown size — the agreed-drop pile is never sampled.
findings.what_it_would_change: Whatever recall harness the funnel gets must sample the DROPPED pile, not only re-score the kept pile. The project already has the right shape for this in src/bad_research/grounding/recall_harness.py — it separates AFFIRMATIVE CATCH from ESCALATE-ONLY and refuses to credit a deferral as a catch (module docstring, lines 15–26; REGRESSION_FLOOR = 1.0 at line 291). That harness is pointed at claim grounding. Point the same structure at Stage E.

findings.claim: What actually predicts a false exclusion is under-DESCRIPTION, not low quality. Abstracts that insufficiently reported study information were falsely excluded 18.4% of the time (95% CI 14.6–22.8) versus 6.0% (4.4–8.3) for those that reported sufficiently; not reporting the study design, 15.4% vs 9.4%. By design: NRSI 19.6% (12.7–28.8), ITS 12.7%, RCT 9.3% (7.5–11.7), NRCT 6.7%. The paper's own explanation is that this tracks reporting-guideline adherence (CONSORT for RCTs), not study design as such.
findings.evidence: Gartlehner-derived meta-epidemiological analysis, BMC Med Res Methodol 2026, PMC13182097, Abstract + Results + Discussion. 924 decisions on 73 studies by 260 reviewers; 826 correct inclusions, 98 false exclusions (10.6%). Elsewhere in the same authors' systematic review: up to 8% falsely excluded for uninformative titles/abstracts, and 11% of eligible non-English studies falsely excluded.
findings.accretes: No — but it names the accretion target. It says a filter's blind spot is a property of genre convention in the candidate's packaging, which means the fix is corpus-specific and learnable rather than a universal rule.
findings.false_negative_cost: A filter reading surface descriptions preferentially deletes work that follows a different (or no) reporting convention — the outsider, the non-English source, the observational study, the record from before the convention existed. Combine with the time-skew in finding 2 and the shape is consistent across two independent datasets: filters kill the differently-packaged, not the wrong.
findings.what_it_would_change: Stop treating a thin or oddly-shaped candidate description as evidence against the candidate. Make 'insufficiently described' a route to ABSTAIN, not to REJECT — which is the same conclusion the 400-char rule reaches from the shipped side. The field's operative decision rule is stated plainly in this paper: 'only exclude studies if they are certain. In cases where there is uncertainty due to missing information in the abstract, it may be prudent to order the full paper.'

findings.claim: Time-on-decision as a confidence proxy is a global null that INVERTS by subgroup. Pooled: median 27.0s for a correct inclusion vs 28.0s for a false exclusion — no discrimination at all. Split: native English reviewers made false exclusions FASTER than correct inclusions (18s vs 27s; 84.6% within 50s), non-natives SLOWER (34s vs 28s; 59.7%); researchers 19s vs 31s; students 61s vs 36s. A pooled 'fast decision = suspect' rule is exactly backwards for half the population.
findings.evidence: BMC Med Res Methodol 2026, PMC13182097, §Time for decisions, Figs. 6–8, Table 2. Same paper, Table 2: reviewers self-rating topic expertise 'Very good' were 12.5% of those who falsely excluded ≥1 abstract but only 4.0% of those who correctly included all — small n (5 vs 4), but the direction is confidence-correlates-with-error, not with accuracy.
findings.accretes: No. It is a warning about a signal a system would naturally reach for. It accretes only in the negative sense: you cannot use effort-spent as a quality proxy until you know which population the decider is in.
findings.false_negative_cost: Unmeasured, and the paper cannot measure it — it is a warning about instrument validity, not a cost estimate. The relevant cost is that a plausible meta-rule ('flag fast rejects for re-review') would, on this data, re-review the wrong half.
findings.what_it_would_change: Do not add a latency/token-spend confidence signal to the funnel's reject path without first checking it splits the same direction in every candidate class. The related operational constant that IS actionable: this literature recommends capping abstract screening at three hours per day per reviewer to limit fatigue — a per-agent throughput cap, not a per-decision one.

findings.claim: Popularity and journal rank are not used as a noise proxy in this field, and the one time it was tested it came back null. In 924 screening decisions, the proportions of false exclusions and correct inclusions were 'similar' across both Medline indexation status and SCImago Journal Rank. Where popularity DOES get used — the citation graph as a retrieval route — it inverts: automated citation searching simulated over 27 systematic reviews on OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar achieved median recall 35.79% (IQR 33.46), median precision 2.57%, median F3 0.028; it beat the reference Boolean search on precision and F1 (p<0.05) and LOST on recall and F3 (p<0.05).
findings.evidence: Null result: BMC Med Res Methodol 2026, PMC13182097, §Journal characteristics + Table 1. Citation-graph inversion: Res Synth Methods 2025, PMC12621532, §4.3–4.4. Reproducibility failure of popularity-ranked engines: Gusenbauer & Haddaway 2020, Res Synth Methods, PMC7079055 §3.4 — of 28 academic search systems only Google Scholar and WorldWideScience failed to return identical results for repeated identical queries, Google Scholar also 'failed all or all but one of the Boolean tests', and only 14 of 28 systems qualify as principal search sources (Google Scholar is not among them).
findings.accretes: No — and the absence is the finding. The field deliberately does not let audience size stand in for relevance, and it rejects the popularity-ranked engine at the level of the ENGINE (non-reproducible, Boolean-noncompliant, capped result sets) rather than at the level of individual results.
findings.false_negative_cost: Using citation-graph popularity as a primary filter costs about two-thirds of recall (35.79% median). The field's response is to demote it to a supplementary method, never a gate — and the same paper notes recall was best for 'signpost' seed types (consensus statements, frameworks, guidelines), i.e. the graph route preferentially finds the already-canonical.
findings.what_it_would_change: src/bad_research/funnel/rank.py:36-54 fuses ~100 queries × providers with RRF k=60 and makes cross-query consensus deliberately UNCAPPED, on the stated grounds that appearing in every list is 'the strongest un-read relevance evidence the funnel can observe'. Against Gusenbauer that is provider-side popularity smuggled in as agreement: the same engine returning the same URL for 100 queries is one observation, not 100. Cap the per-provider contribution, or verify the providers are reproducible before treating repeat sightings as independent evidence. Note this is a RANKING signal, so its failure mode is soft — the fix is bounded, not urgent.

findings.claim: There is a published spec for what makes a stopping rule legitimate, and its third clause invalidates every hand-tuned threshold: a rule must (1) target a user-set recall level, (2) emit a calibrated confidence — at 95%, it must trigger before the target is met no more than 5% of the time — and (3) be 'free from additional parameters that require knowledge of the screening outcomes to be set effectively'. 'Stop after X consecutive irrelevant' fails (3), because the user has no way to know the right X a priori. Meanwhile the field's own guidance has not caught up: Cochrane Handbook 6.4 still does not recommend early stopping, and PRISMA 2020 requires only 'details of automation tools used', with no rationale for the stopping decision — while 46 screening tools shipped as of January 2024, many with ML prioritisation and no validated stopping rule.
findings.evidence: Syst Rev 2024, PMC11583672 (multi-author commentary), §'The state of early stopping' and Recommendation 1 / Fig. 1. Local copy: scratchpad/pmc/PMC11583672.txt.
findings.accretes: Clause (3) is the accretion test itself. A rule whose parameter can only be set by knowing the answer cannot improve with context — it can only be retro-fitted. A rule stated in terms of a target and a confidence gets sharper automatically as the seen set grows.
findings.false_negative_cost: Unmeasured across the tool ecosystem, and the commentary says so directly: evaluations use different metrics, independent assessments are missing, and reported reliability may come from over-fitting the stopping criterion to the experimental setup. Tens of thousands of live reviews are stopping on unvalidated rules.
findings.what_it_would_change: Audit every constant in the funnel against clause (3). Ask of each: could I have set this without already knowing the answer for this run? `redundancy_overlap`, the top-N read budget, and `min_chars=300` all fail that test as currently justified. Constants that fail it should be replaced by a target-plus-confidence formulation or explicitly logged as pragmatic-and-unvalidated, which is what the commentary asks of tool builders.

findings.claim: The recall/precision exchange rate for pushing a classifier to a recall target is steep and measured: the same ensemble model scored recall 0.902 / precision 0.953 at a balanced 0.5 cutoff, and after moving the cutoff to hit recall 0.99, precision fell to 0.353 / 0.483 / 0.400 across three datasets. Roughly 9 points of recall cost 55–60 points of precision. In practice this is accepted because the base rate is brutal: standard database retrieval yields only ~7% true RCTs, and ML-assisted double screening measured recall 0.998 versus 0.919 for a single human reviewer, at 45.4% average labour saving (74.4% in a stepwise configuration).
findings.evidence: Res Synth Methods 2025, PMC12527483, §3.1.1–3.1.2 and Abstract/Highlights. Corroborating human baseline from a separate group: single-reviewer benchmark of recall 0.86 / specificity 0.79, in Syst Rev 2026 PMC13248334 (which compares four TF-IDF supervised baselines against Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on six SR datasets).
findings.accretes: No — a static threshold sweep. But it quantifies the price of the accreting rules in findings 4 and 5: those mechanisms exist precisely so you don't have to pay this precision cost on every candidate, only on the ones the guarantee still needs.
findings.false_negative_cost: Explicit in the cutoff choice. The field never picks the cutoff from the precision side, and never optimises F1 for screening — the reported metric is F3, which weights recall 3× precision. That alone is a transferable constant: evidence synthesis has settled on a 3:1 asymmetry between missing something and reading something useless.
findings.what_it_would_change: If badresearch ever scores candidates with a model, set the cutoff by recall target and report the precision it costs, rather than picking a balanced threshold. And adopt F3, not F1, as the funnel's headline metric — the current codebase reports neither.

negative_results: Popularity is not a screening feature in this field, at all. `grep -c -i -E "citation count|impact factor|h-index|altmetric" pmc/*.txt` over 16 full-text screening-methodology papers (~1.06 MB) returned 0 for 15 of them; the single non-zero file (PMC9291810) is a librarianship commentary, not a screening study. The only popularity variable ever tested as a screening covariate — SCImago Journal Rank plus Medline indexation, in PMC13182097 — was tested as a predictor of screening ERROR and found null.

Nobody measures the downstream cost of a miss. `grep -c -i -E "change[d]? the (conclusion|finding|result)|impact on the (findings|conclusion|results)|altered the (conclusion|effect estimate)" pmc/*.txt` returned exactly one non-zero file out of 16 (Waffenschmidt 2019, PMC6599339, and only for 7 screenings). Fifteen papers report sensitivity/recall and stop there. The field measures the rate of false negatives well and their consequence almost never.

badresearch has no recall instrumentation on its candidate filter. `grep -rniE "recall|sensitivity|false.?negative|missed" --include="*.py" src/` returns only: `neural_recall` (a retrieval-mode config flag, config.py:51/91/109), `grounding/recall_harness.py` (which measures claim-grounding guards, a different stage), and prose in core/hooks.py. Nothing in src/bad_research/funnel/ measures what Stage E drops. `grep -rncE "false.?negative" --include="*.py" src/` hits only recitation.py, checks/__init__.py and checks/discriminate.py — the output-quality lane, never the intake lane.

badresearch's funnel filter has no abstain path. src/bad_research/funnel/filter.py:71-75 is a binary list comprehension: a candidate whose reject-reason is not None is dropped, full stop. `grep -rniE "abstain|escalat|uncertain|defer_to_human|needs_review" --include="*.py" src/` finds the escalate concept ONLY inside grounding/recall_harness.py, where it is correctly implemented and correctly not credited as a catch. The right pattern already exists in the repo, at the wrong stage.

Silver could not reach the two BMC/Springer article pages I first targeted — both returned 'A required part of this site couldn't load. This may be due to a browser extension, network issues, or browser settings' from a headless session. This is worth recording because it is the failure mode the brief warns about: an empty or interstitial fetch that reads as a page. The recovery was the Europe PMC REST API (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/<PMCID>/fullTextXML), which returns publisher JATS XML verbatim, is free and keyless, and is a better source than a rendered page for anything with a PMCID.
open_questions: What is the concordant false-negative rate — the share of candidates that BOTH readers (or both models) wrongly reject? Wang 2020 states outright that its design cannot measure it, and I found no study that does. Every recall figure in this lane is conditioned on at least one reader having said yes. This is the single largest unmeasured quantity in the field and it is exactly the class the owner's project is exposed to.

Does the calibration-sample mechanism (finding 5) survive when the corpus is heterogeneous? Every instance I found calibrates against one review's criteria over one topically-coherent record set. A badresearch run fans ~100 queries across providers and topics; whether a threshold fit on a 19% sample generalises across that spread is untested here, and the topic-dependence of human error (5.76%–21.11% by clinical area, Wang 2020 Table 2) suggests it may not.

The hypergeometric stopping criterion (finding 4) assumes the unseen pool is a fixed, enumerable population — true for a database export, false for a live web funnel where new candidates arrive as queries are issued. What the criterion becomes when the denominator is open is not addressed in PMC7700715 and I found no follow-up that addresses it. This is the main obstacle to importing the mechanism directly.

Nobody has measured how often a model REFUSES a candidate (safety filter, content policy) rather than judging it, or what topics that concentrates in. The one data point I have — Gemini Pro 1.0 declining 15 of 2,043 records on 'incest', 'pedophilia', 'child trafficking' (PMC13263951 Step 5) — is reported as an incidental annoyance, not as a measured bias. It is a 0.7% deletion rate concentrated entirely in one research area.

Whether reviewer/model DISAGREEMENT is itself a usable signal about the candidate rather than about the reader. The full-agreement approach throws discordant cases to humans; nobody asks whether the discordant 19% are systematically the interesting ones. Gartlehner 2026 hints at it — false exclusions concentrate in under-described records, which are also the ones readers would disagree about — but nobody has tested 'disagreement predicts value'.

findings.claim: The shipped mechanism for rejecting a candidate is a cheap model's own top-k list re-scored by an expensive model used ONLY as a veto, with two hard thresholds: keep as negative if cross-encoder score < 0.1, promote to positive if > 0.9. Skipping the veto is worse than doing no mining at all: MS MARCO MRR@10 goes 32.39 (in-batch baseline) -> 26.03 (raw hard negatives) -> 36.38 (denoised hard negatives) -> 37.02 (+ pseudo-labelled augmentation).
findings.evidence: RocketQA, Qu et al. NAACL 2021, arXiv:2010.08191, Table 3 and Sec. 4.2.2 (read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2010.08191, saved line 212-214 for Table 3, line 180 for the 0.1/0.9 thresholds and the ">90%" manual accuracy of the selected data, line 236 for the audit).
findings.accretes: Yes, and it is the clearest accretion loop in the literature. STEP 3 re-mines negatives from the CURRENT retriever's output and filters them with a cross-encoder trained on accumulated labels; STEP 4 then uses the same cross-encoder to pseudo-label 1.7M previously unlabelled questions and feeds them back as training data. The gate is a learned artifact that gets re-applied to the generator's own fresh output every round, not a rule list.
findings.false_negative_cost: Measured explicitly and it is the paper's founding observation: they manually examined the top-retrieved-but-unlabelled passages for 100 questions and found ~70% were actually positive or highly relevant. MS MARCO has 1.1 labelled positives per question against 8.8M passages. Figure 5 shows the denoiser filters MORE passages at LOWER ranks, i.e. the false-negative density is not monotone in score. Table 4 names two concrete wrongly-rejected passages (a kHz/MHz answer at rank 14, an Achilles-tendon test at rank 9). This is the only paper in my sample that names casualties.
findings.what_it_would_change: Never let the sweep's own top-k become 'rejected' without a second, different-architecture reader passing over it. Adopt the asymmetric two-threshold gate rather than one cutoff: a band in the middle stays UNDECIDED rather than being deleted. And expect the ~70% figure to hold: most of what a first-pass sweep ranks high and you did not label is probably real.

findings.claim: A filter trained on a FROZEN set of negatives has no performance guarantee at all — the bound collapses to MRR ~ 1/|C| — and empirically it buys top-of-list precision by destroying recall: BM25-mined static negatives give MRR@10 0.309 / R@100 0.813 against random negatives' 0.301 / 0.853 on MS MARCO passage, and 0.539 nDCG@10 / R@100 0.362 against 0.572 / 0.464 on the document task (a 10-point recall collapse).
findings.evidence: Zhan et al., 'Optimizing Dense Retrieval Model Training with Hard Negatives', SIGIR 2021, arXiv:2104.08051. Worst-case bound: Sec. 5.1 ('In the worst case, MRR is approximately 1/|C| ... we believe it is risky to use static hard negative sampling'). Numbers: Table 2 rows BM25 Neg / Rand Neg. Read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.08051 (saved zhan.txt, 504 lines).
findings.accretes: Only if the negatives are re-mined against the CURRENT model each step. That is the paper's whole result: 'dynamic' hard negatives (ADORE re-retrieves per training iteration) are bounded and safe; 'static' ones (mined once by BM25 or a warm-up model) are unbounded and unstable. ANCE's compromise is an asynchronous index refresh every 10k training batches with a 1:1 trainer:inferencer GPU split (arXiv:2007.00808, Sec. 4 / implementation details).
findings.false_negative_cost: Measured as an aggregate recall drop (R@100 0.853 -> 0.813 passage; 0.464 -> 0.362 doc) and never as an identity. Also note the tail effect they DO measure: 0.2% of queries (pairwise errors >= 10^5) contribute 60% of total pairwise error (Fig. 3 / Sec. 8.1) — a filter tuned on mean error is hijacked by 0.2% of the input.
findings.what_it_would_change: Two things. (1) Any reject-list built from an early sweep must be re-derived after the run learns something, not carried forward; a frozen reject-list is the failure mode with no lower bound. (2) Report top-k precision and deep recall separately on every filter change — they move in opposite directions, and a filter that improves your top-10 is probably deleting 10 points of reachable recall you never see.

findings.claim: The cheap first stage's REJECTION CRITERION is structurally different from the expensive stage's scoring criterion, so it permanently deletes exactly what the expensive stage was best at. Stated as a design rule and quantified: BM25 requires at least one exact query term; recall@1000 is 85.7% (Anserini) vs 81.5% (Microsoft) for the *same* BM25 function, differing only in tokenization/stopwords/stemming.
findings.evidence: Nogueira, Yang, Cho, Lin, 'Multi-Stage Document Ranking with BERT', arXiv:1910.14424. Design rule at saved multistage.txt line 46: 'BM25 is based on exact term matches, and all candidates must contain at least one term from the user's query. However, since later BERT stages operate in continuous vector spaces, they have the ability to identify relevant candidates that do not have many matching terms. Thus, it is critical in H0 to optimize for recall ... precision is less of a concern because non-relevant documents can be discarded by later stages.' Recall numbers at line 162. Cascade constants k0=1000, k1=50 at line 118. Cost accounting at line 166: duoBERT considers top 50 from H1 and 'requires an additional 50x49 BERT inferences' for +0.5 MRR@10, against monoBERT's 1000 inferences for +17.5.
findings.accretes: No — fixed constants (1000, 50), tuned once. This is the null result for stage sizing. The only adaptivity they offer is 'early exits' for easy queries, cited to Cambazoglu et al. 2010 but not implemented or measured here.
findings.false_negative_cost: Reported once as a single aggregate (85.7% recall@1000) and then never mentioned again in 312 lines. The 4.2-point gap between two implementations of the same function means implementation trivia silently deletes ~4% of all reachable answers and no downstream metric would reveal it.
findings.what_it_would_change: Budget the cascade by marginal points-per-inference, not by intuition: stage 1 bought 17.5 MRR points for 1000 inferences (0.0175/inf); the final expensive stage bought 0.5 points for 2450 inferences (0.0002/inf), an 87x worse rate. And pick the cheap filter so its rejection criterion is NOT a proper subset of the expensive reader's — otherwise the pipeline's ceiling is the cheap filter's blind spot, permanently.

findings.claim: Learned per-query truncation ('decide how many candidates to pay for') does NOT beat a hardcoded constant. Across 8 truncation methods, 3 retrievers and 2 re-rankers on TREC-DL 19/20: with a strong first stage (SPLADE++ or RepLLaMA), Fixed-k=20 gives the best effectiveness/efficiency trade-off in every scenario and supervised methods' gains are not statistically significant. The headroom is real and unreachable: an oracle cut-off shows ~30% of queries need NO re-ranking at all (RepLLaMA first stage), ~5% with BM25.
findings.evidence: Meng, Arabzadeh, Askari, Aliannejadi, de Rijke, 'Ranked List Truncation for LLM-based Re-Ranking', SIGIR 2024, arXiv:2404.18185. Lessons paragraph (saved rlt.txt line 53): 'supervised RLT methods do not show a clear advantage over using a fixed re-ranking depth ... a fixed re-ranking depth of 20 can already yield an excellent effectiveness/efficiency trade-off'. Oracle 30%/5% at line 93. Best supervised result: Choppy(beta=0) matches Fixed-k(1000) nDCG@10 at 69% of cost, AttnCut at 86% (line 279). Error analysis line 53: 'supervised RLT methods tend to fail to predict when not to carry out re-ranking'.
findings.accretes: No, and this is the measured null result the brief asked for. The supervised truncators are trained offline on a fixed label set and never improve in-run; the authors attribute their failure partly to 'a lack of training data'. Their unsupervised competitor Surprise (arXiv:2010.09797) sets its threshold from a Cramer-von-Mises statistic and has no tunable hyperparameter at all — and is competitive.
findings.false_negative_cost: NOT MEASURED. The word 'recall' appears zero times in 578 lines of a paper entirely about what to discard before the expensive model. They do control for the adjacent confound (judged@10 is 95.35% at fixed k=1000 vs 96.05% at oracle cut-offs) but never ask what the truncation deleted.
findings.what_it_would_change: Do not build a learned 'is this worth reading' scorer first. Ship a constant k, measure the oracle gap by occasionally reading past k, and only then decide whether a learner can close it. Also: the value of ANY truncator is a function of the generator's quality — with a good first stage, k=20 is optimal and a learner is pure overhead. If the sweep improves, the filter's job shrinks.

findings.claim: The accreting filter that demonstrably beats the static one is Continuous Active Learning (relevance feedback on the top-scored, retrained every batch) — and the comparison is run with the static learner's training cost set to ZERO and it still loses. Concrete constants: seed = ONE relevant document; 100 randomly drawn documents presumptively labelled 'not relevant' each iteration to give the SVM a boundary; batch size starts at 1 and grows by ceil(B/10), which makes the run O(n log n + T(n)) instead of the O(n^2) that batch-size-1 would cost.
findings.evidence: Cormack & Grossman, 'Autonomy and Reliability of Continuous Active Learning for Technology-Assisted Review', arXiv:1504.06868, Secs. 3.3.2-3.3.3 and 4.3. Read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1504.06868. The sunk-cost comparison: 'Under the SPL model, all the categorization results are inferior to the baseline. Perhaps surprisingly, the vast majority are also inferior under the sunk-cost model' (i.e. even when the statically-trained classifier's labels are free). Validated on 804,401 RCV1-v2 docs x 103 subjects, 4 real legal matters, TREC-6 ad hoc (50 topics), TREC-2002 Filtering (50 topics). Feature-engineering control: their SVM reproduces Lewis et al.'s F1=0.607 at F1=0.608.
findings.accretes: Yes — this IS the accretion mechanism, and it is measured against its non-accreting twins. CAL (feed back the top-scored) > SAL (uncertainty sampling) > SPL (train once, apply once), consistently, per-topic, at every recall level 0.1 through 0.9, sign test P ~ 0.000.
findings.false_negative_cost: Measured as gain curves at every recall level, not a single operating point — that is the discipline. And the failure mode is characterised rather than hidden: 'when Auto TAR fails, it seems to do so spectacularly, retrieving a near-vacuous number of documents. Such a situation would be readily apparent, and would signal to the user to abandon the effort and start again with another seed.' A filter whose failure looks like success is the dangerous one; theirs does not.
findings.what_it_would_change: Structure the run as CAL, not as screen-then-read: one confirmed-good source seeds it, you read the current top-scored batch, every judgement immediately retrains the scorer, and batch size grows ~10% per round so early rounds are nearly one-at-a-time (max learning) and late rounds are cheap. Bootstrap the negative class with ~100 random unread candidates presumptively labelled bad rather than waiting for real negatives. And note the counter-intuitive one: uncertainty sampling (the textbook active-learning move) LOSES to plain greedy exploitation when the goal is high recall on a rare class.

findings.claim: Nobody measures false negatives because measuring them is arithmetically prohibitive at low base rates: a simple random sample that estimates recall to +/-0.05 at 95% confidence needs roughly 385 RELEVANT documents in it, so at 1% prevalence you must review ~38,500 documents just to audit your filter.
findings.evidence: Yang, Lewis, Frieder, 'Heuristic Stopping Rules for Technology-Assisted Review', DocEng 2021, arXiv:2106.09871, Sec. 3.2 (read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2106.09871): 'the size of a sample necessary to estimate recall with a given confidence is inversely proportional to the prevalence ... estimating recall with a margin of error of 0.05 and a confidence level of 95% requires a simple random sample containing roughly 385 relevant documents. If the prevalence of relevant documents was 1%, one could need on average a sample size of 38,500 documents.'
findings.accretes: The stopping rules built on top of it do. Their MaxProb rule stops when the max predicted probability among unreviewed items falls to <= 0.1 — chosen because 1/p is the expected number of documents you must read to find one more good one, so 0.1 means 'nine duds per hit', an explicit marginal-cost cutoff that moves as the model improves. The Knee method reads the shape of the gain curve (max perpendicular distance from the chord) rather than any fixed score.
findings.false_negative_cost: Measured directly and asymmetrically. They reject 'reliability' (fraction of runs meeting the recall target) as gameable — 'a null stopping rule that never stops the process would have perfect but uninformative reliability' — and use MSE of recall-at-stopping, which penalises overshoot and undershoot. The undershoot penalty is the number of extra documents you'd have to read, in the model's own order, to reach target: worked example, 10,000 docs / 1,000 relevant / target 0.5, stopped at 2,001 reviewed with 300 found -> penalty 2,300, total cost 4,301. Target-agnostic rules overshoot badly at low targets: Knee MSE 0.522 at target 0.1 vs 0.029 at 0.9; Budget 0.546 vs 0.019.
findings.what_it_would_change: Stop asking 'is this filter accurate' and start asking 'what is my marginal cost of the next real find'. Instrument the run with 1/p: when the best unread candidate scores below ~0.1 calibrated probability, you are paying nine reads per hit and should stop or change lanes. And if you ever want a defensible recall number, price it first — at 1% prevalence it costs 38,500 reads, which is almost certainly more than the run itself.

findings.claim: A high-recall screening pipeline has a NAMED, PARAMETERISED false-negative cost function, and the standard operating points are published: recall target 80% in eDiscovery, 95% in medical systematic reviews. Cost = alpha_p*t_p + alpha_n*t_n + beta_p*m_p + beta_n*m_n, where t are docs read to train the filter and m are docs still needing review to hit target; benchmarked under (1,1,1,1) 'uniform' and (10,10,1,1) 'expensive'.
findings.evidence: Mao, Koopman, Zuccon, 'A Reproducibility Study of Goldilocks: Just-Right Tuning of BERT for TAR', ECIR 2024, arXiv:2401.08104, Sec. 3 metrics (read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2401.08104). Corpora: RCV1-v2 (45 categories binned by prevalence x difficulty), Jeb Bush (44 topics, 274,124 unique emails), CLEF TAR 2017-2019 (6 collections, 30,521-218,484 docs each).
findings.accretes: The pipeline does (active learning, batch 200 for RCV1/Jeb Bush, 25 for CLEF). But the finding that matters is where accretion FAILS: out of domain, plain logistic regression beats further-pre-trained BERT by ~20% R-Precision (LR 0.892 vs BERT-best 0.706 on Jeb Bush) and BERT costs 2.7x-6.5x the LR baseline. Worse, BERT is worst exactly in the Hard x Rare bin — 1.279 to 2.466x LR cost at EVERY pre-training epoch setting (Table 2). Runtime: LR 0.4 min/run vs BERT 56-62 min/run.
findings.false_negative_cost: Fully priced, and the pricing is what exposes the heavy filter: under 'expensive' training cost the sophisticated filter is a net loss because the documents it burns learning are documents it did not find. Also: the 'Goldilocks epoch' did not reproduce (original said 5, reproduction found 10; per-bin epochs differ), and 'an incorrect setting makes the BERT classifier underperform a baseline logistic regression, even on in-domain tasks'.
findings.what_it_would_change: Adopt their cost algebra verbatim: count reads spent teaching the filter separately from reads spent finding things, and weight them differently. Then apply the empirical warning — for RARE and HARD targets (your exact case), the heavy learned filter is measurably worse and 140x slower than a trivial linear one, and its one critical hyperparameter is not reproducible across corpora.

findings.claim: A score threshold is only meaningful against the negative distribution it was calibrated on. Changing ONLY the negative sampler at test time (train negatives=BM25, test negatives=random) blows up expected calibration error by 25x: ECE 0.002 -> 0.050. Domain shift alone costs ~9x: 0.003 -> 0.028.
findings.evidence: Penha & Hauff, 'On the Calibration and Uncertainty of Neural Learning to Rank Models', EACL 2021, arXiv:2101.04356, Table 1 (read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2101.04356). UDC-trained row: in-domain R10@1 0.834 / ECE 0.002; NS_random 0.318 / 0.050; NS_sentenceBERT 0.182 / 0.045. MANTiS-trained row: 0.615/0.003 in-domain -> 0.422/0.028 on UDC. Figure 2 separately shows calibration degrading as the test set is made more unbalanced (more non-relevant per query) than the balanced training set — the base-rate effect on the threshold.
findings.accretes: Partially and unreliably. Their fix (ensembles / MC-dropout to get a predictive distribution) reduces ECE by up to 56.14% on some train/test pairs but makes it 25.05% WORSE on others (Table 2, MSDialog row). Uncertainty estimates did buy something downstream: +33% average F1 on predicting 'no correct answer exists in this candidate list'.
findings.false_negative_cost: Not framed as false negatives, but the mechanism is exactly the owner's anti-bot case: a page that is real, accurate and quotable but off-topic is a NEW KIND OF NEGATIVE. The filter's threshold was never calibrated against it, so the probability it emits is uninterpretable, and it will be wrong in an unknown direction.
findings.what_it_would_change: Treat the reject threshold as belonging to a (source-population, negative-type) pair, not to the filter. When a new class of plausible-but-wrong content appears — an anti-bot decoy, an LLM-generated near-miss — the old cutoff is invalid, not merely imprecise. Cheapest instrument: keep a small held-out set of each known negative TYPE and recompute ECE per type; a type whose ECE has moved is a type whose threshold must be re-set. And note the base-rate coupling: a filter calibrated on balanced data is miscalibrated the moment real prevalence drops.

findings.claim: Using rank/engagement as a relevance proxy does not merely add noise — it converges to the WRONG ranker, and the error is asymptotic, so more data never fixes it. Naive rank-SVM trained on clicks has an essentially FLAT learning curve; propensity-weighted training approaches the full-information skyline.
findings.evidence: Joachims, Swaminathan, Schnabel, 'Unbiased Learning-to-Rank with Biased Feedback', WSDM 2017, arXiv:1608.04468, Sec. 7.2-7.4 (read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1608.04468): 'Naive SVM-Rank cannot make effective use of additional data and its learning curve is essentially flat ... estimation error is dominated by asymptotic bias due to biased clicks, which does not decrease with more data'. Bias model p_r = (1/rank)^eta; at eta=1, rank 10 has a 10% examination probability and ~33% of clicks are on irrelevant results (eps_-=0.1); at eps_-=0.3, 59.8% of all clicks are on irrelevant documents. Live deployment on an operational scientific-article search engine: 21 days, 5,437 training clicks, interleaving vs Naive 95 wins / 60 losses / 102 ties, p=0.006.
findings.accretes: Yes, but only after you pay for a causal correction. The propensities are estimated by a swap intervention (move the item at rank r to a landmark rank k and compare click rates) run on a SMALL subset — the training data itself needs no randomisation. Without that intervention, accumulating more engagement data actively entrenches the bias.
findings.false_negative_cost: The whole paper is the false-negative story: a good item that was never shown high is never clicked, and the naive learner reads that as evidence it is bad. Crucially they measure the misspecification asymmetry — 'overestimating small propensities is tolerable ... underestimating small propensities can be harmful'. Err toward assuming an item WAS seen and rejected on merit only when you are sure; otherwise assume it was never seen.
findings.what_it_would_change: Direct answer to Q4. Any popularity, citation, star-count or 'appears near the top of search' signal must enter as an inverse-propensity WEIGHT, never as a feature or a filter. Practically: down-weight a candidate's absence of endorsement by the probability it could have been endorsed given its obscurity, and when in doubt, over-estimate that probability. A run that ranks by popularity will get more confident and no more correct as it gathers data.

findings.claim: Venue/citation rank as a quality proxy inverts hard: of 18 deep-learning top-n recommendation papers from KDD/SIGIR/WWW/RecSys 2015-2018, only 7 (39%) were reproducible, 6 of those 7 were beaten by simple tuned kNN or graph baselines, and in one case 'a non-personalized method that recommends the most popular items to everyone was the best one in terms of certain accuracy measures'.
findings.evidence: Ferrari Dacrema, Cremonesi, Jannach, 'Are We Really Making Much Progress? A Worrying Analysis of Recent Neural Recommendation Approaches', RecSys 2019, arXiv:1907.06902, Sec. 2.1 / Table 1 (7/18 total; RecSys 1/7 = 14%) and Sec. 3 (read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1907.06902). They quote Armstrong et al. 2009's earlier ad-hoc-retrieval finding that reported improvements 'don't add up', so this is a replicated failure mode, not a one-off.
findings.accretes: No — and worse, it degrades: they identify 'establishment of weak methods as new baselines' as a mechanism, so each accumulated round of published work makes the next comparison easier to win. An accreting filter that treats prior acceptance as evidence gets systematically worse over time.
findings.false_negative_cost: Not measured as false negatives — nobody asked which unpublished or unfashionable method would have won. That absence is itself the finding: the field measures whether the accepted thing is good and never whether the rejected thing was better.
findings.what_it_would_change: Second half of the Q4 answer. Do not let 'published at a strong venue', 'highly cited', or 'many stars' promote a candidate past reading. But keep the inverse: the trivially popular baseline is a real contender and belongs in the comparison as a CONTROL, because it sometimes wins outright. Every filter you build should be scored against 'take the most popular thing' before you believe it.

findings.claim: The ceiling on any filter's measurable accuracy is the self-consistency of the judgement it imitates, and that number is roughly a coin flip: assessors shown a document a SECOND time agreed with their own first label only 52% of the time; two independent groups of trained TREC assessors agree at Cohen's kappa 0.52; labelling web pages for spam gets kappa 0.56.
findings.evidence: Thomas, Spielman, Craswell, Mitra (Microsoft/Bing), 'Large Language Models can Accurately Predict Searcher Preferences', SIGIR 2024, arXiv:2309.10621, Sec. 4.1 related-work paragraph (read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2309.10621), citing Scholer et al. 2013 (52% self-agreement), Cormack et al. 1998 (kappa=0.52 between two trained assessor groups), Castillo et al. 2006 (kappa=0.56 for spam), Hersh et al. 1994 (kappa=0.41 on OHSUMED). In the same paper, the SAME model on the SAME 3,000 query:document pairs swings from kappa 0.20 (prompt 'R--M') to 0.64 (prompt '-DNA-') purely on prompt features, and the authors warn performance 'varies unpredictably with simple paraphrases'.
findings.accretes: Their proposal is exactly an accretion mechanism with a fixed anchor: collect a SMALL set of first-party gold labels from the person who actually had the need, then use it to SELECT the model and prompt, then scale. The gold set is the invariant; the filter is the thing that gets tuned against it. Note the actor and interest — this is Bing, and Figure 1 is a cost/accuracy chart for replacing crowd labellers, so treat the 'LLMs beat every human population' headline with suspicion; the borrowed inter-assessor numbers are from third parties and are the durable part.
findings.false_negative_cost: They name the structural version: 'If workers are systematically misunderstanding searcher needs (i.e., the labels are biased) this cannot be fixed by getting more data' — the same asymptotic-bias argument Joachims proves for clicks, arrived at independently. A systematically wrong filter does not converge.
findings.what_it_would_change: Two operational consequences. (1) Before trusting any measured filter accuracy, establish the ceiling: re-judge a sample of your own past accept/reject decisions blind and see how often you agree with yourself. If it is near 52%, differences smaller than that between filter variants are noise. (2) A prompt-defined filter is not one filter — a paraphrase is a different classifier with a 3x range in agreement. Pin the prompt, version it, and re-measure on any edit.

findings.claim: The 'right answer' a filter is trained to keep is often not the best answer available: on MS MARCO, crowd assessors prefer a neural ranker's top passage over the official gold label 58.6% of the time when they disagree, the official gold labels win only 46.6% of their head-to-head pairings, and a PERFECT ranker under the official labels scores MRR@10 = 0.3320 under preference labels.
findings.evidence: Arabzadeh, Vtyurina, Yan, Clarke, 'Shallow pooling for sparse labels', arXiv:2109.00062, Secs. 3 and 5-6 (read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2109.00062). 6,980 dev queries, 94% with exactly one qrel. Table 1: Category A (ranker agrees with gold) 1,228 vs 640 -> gold preferred 65.7%, used as a control that puts crowdsourcing error at ~33%; Category B (disagree) 2,116 vs 2,996 -> ranker preferred 58.6%. Preference qrels win 91.8% (1,598) of pairings vs original qrels' 46.6% (809). Kendall tau=0.65 between the two evaluations, but the top of the leaderboard reorders and three runs significantly beat a 'perfect' ranking under Bonferroni correction.
findings.accretes: Yes, and the accretion design is cheap and worth stealing: they keep only the CURRENT best-known answer per query and, whenever a ranker surfaces an unjudged item at rank 1, run one head-to-head comparison against the incumbent and replace it if preferred. That is O(1) maintenance per new candidate — no re-pooling, no re-judging the corpus.
findings.false_negative_cost: This is the measurement of it. Everything the filter deleted for 'not matching the known-good exemplar' was scored, and more than half the time the deleted thing was better. They also included the control condition (Category A) so the preference signal cannot be dismissed as crowd noise.
findings.what_it_would_change: Directly addresses 'my false-negative, not their false-positive'. Never encode a fixed exemplar of the good thing and reject by distance from it. Keep a champion-per-slot and let any new candidate challenge it in a single pairwise comparison — pairwise is cheaper and higher-agreement than absolute scoring, and the incumbent gets replaced rather than defended. Also: if your filter is tuned to reproduce a gold set, its measured ceiling is contaminated the moment it becomes better than that gold set.

findings.claim: The diagnostic that separates 'genuinely bad' from 'actually good but unlabelled' is gradient VARIANCE, not score, and the operational rule falls out of it: sample negatives whose relevance score sits NEAR a known positive's score, not at the top of the list. Gradient means decay gently across the top 200 (1.0 -> 0.25) while gradient variances of the top 10 are dramatically larger — because those are false negatives.
findings.evidence: Zhou et al. (Microsoft), 'SimANS: Simple Ambiguous Negatives Sampling for Dense Text Retrieval', EMNLP 2022 industry, arXiv:2210.11773, Sec. 3 'Results and Findings' and Sec. 4.1 (read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2210.11773). Three stated sampling principles: obviously-irrelevant -> sample less (uninformative, near-zero gradient); highly-relevant-looking -> sample less ('positives in disguise'); score close to a positive -> sample more. Implementation: exponential distribution over the top-k with k=100, O(k). Bing production dataset: +2% absolute Hit@5 over top-k hard negatives.
findings.accretes: Yes, structurally — the sampling distribution is defined RELATIVE to the current model's score for a known positive, so it re-centres itself every time the model improves. It is a moving threshold, not a fixed one, and it needs no extra labels.
findings.false_negative_cost: Measured indirectly but honestly: they show that the gradient signature of a false negative (high variance) is theoretically detrimental to convergence and empirically concentrated in the top 10. They do not name individual casualties. Improvements are largest on MS MARCO passage and doc, which they attribute to those being real search logs that 'suffer severely from the false negative problem'.
findings.what_it_would_change: Gives a cheap, label-free rule for the owner's exact failure: apparent depth anti-correlating with sourcing. The most confident-looking rejects in a candidate list are the ones most likely to be real. Rank candidates by |score - score(a known-good exemplar)| and spend reading budget on the band closest to a confirmed find, not on the extremes. The top of your reject list should be treated as UNRESOLVED, not resolved.

findings.claim: In-domain filter accuracy does not predict out-of-domain filter accuracy, and the gap is enormous: across 18 heterogeneous datasets, DPR averages -47.7% against BM25, DeepCT -27.9%, SPARTA -20.3%, ANCE -7.4% — while the untrained lexical baseline holds. The only architecture that generalises is the one that reads query and candidate JOINTLY at scoring time (BM25+CE, +11%, beats BM25 on 16/18) and it costs 6,100ms CPU per query against BM25's 20ms — a 305x price for the thing that works.
findings.evidence: Thakur, Reimers, Ruckle, Srivastava, Gurevych, 'BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models', NeurIPS 2021 D&B, arXiv:2104.08663, Table 2 final row ('Avg. Performance vs. BM25') and the latency table on DBPedia 1M (read at https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.08663; saved beir.txt, 825 lines). Finding 1 verbatim: 'In-domain performance is not a good indicator for out-of-domain generalization. We observe BM25 heavily underperforms neural approaches by 7-18 points on in-domain MS MARCO. However, BEIR reveals it to be a strong baseline for generalization.' BM25+CE fails on exactly the two task-shifted datasets, ArguAna and Touche-2020.
findings.accretes: No, in the direction that matters: the models that compress a candidate into a learned prior (DeepCT, SPARTA, DPR) accreted knowledge of ONE domain and became actively harmful elsewhere. Document expansion (docT5query, +1.6%, beats BM25 on 11/18) accretes safely because it ADDS surface signal rather than replacing the matching function.
findings.false_negative_cost: Not measured as such — zero occurrences of 'false negative' in 825 lines. Reported only as aggregate nDCG@10 deltas. They do note dense retrievers have a length preference (Figure 6: TAS-B favours shorter documents), which is an unmeasured systematic deletion.
findings.what_it_would_change: The cheap pre-read filter should stay dumb and lexical, and the expensive stage should be a joint reader, because that split is what survives distribution shift. Concretely: resist the temptation to train a learned 'source quality' embedding from this run's accumulated context — that is the DPR pattern and it loses 47.7% when the next question is about a different domain. Spend the accumulated context on the JOINT reader's prompt instead, where it is conditioned on the specific candidate rather than baked into a prior.

open_questions: Every accreting filter I found (CAL, ADORE, ANCE, SimANS, RocketQA) accretes over a FIXED information need. None of them handles a run whose question is itself being refined as it reads. Does anything in the TAR literature cover topic drift mid-review, or is 'the target moved' simply outside the model? Cormack & Grossman's failure mode ('abandon and reseed') suggests they treat it as unrecoverable.

Is there any measurement of first-stage recall where the LOST items were subsequently read and characterised? Every number I found (BM25 recall@1000 = 85.7%; DPR -47.7%) is an aggregate against an existing label set, which cannot see items no system in the pool ever retrieved. The Shallow Pooling method (champion + single pairwise challenge) is the only maintenance loop I found that could in principle surface them, and it only operates on rank 1.

The anti-bot case the owner raised is formally a NEW NEGATIVE CLASS appearing at test time. Penha & Hauff measure that this destroys calibration (ECE 0.002 -> 0.050 on a negative-sampler swap alone) but their fix (ensembles) helps inconsistently and sometimes hurts. Is there any work on DETECTING that the negative distribution has shifted, as opposed to being robust to it? That detector, not a better classifier, seems like the actual missing instrument.

Cormack & Grossman's CAL beats uncertainty sampling (SAL) for high-recall retrieval, but Mao/Koopman/Zuccon found uncertainty sampling wins on R-Precision while losing on cost. Whether greedy exploitation or uncertainty sampling is right appears to depend on the cost structure, and I did not find a paper that states the crossover condition explicitly.

I have no evidence at all on whether reading budget is better spent going DEEP on few candidates or SHALLOW on many, at fixed total cost. The cascade papers fix depth exogenously (k0=1000, k1=50) and the RLT paper shows learned depth does not beat a constant, but neither compares 'read 20 candidates carefully' against 'skim 200'. This is the question I would send the next lane at.

Actor/interest check I could not resolve: the LLM-judge result (arXiv:2309.10621) is Bing arguing that LLMs can replace their crowd labellers, and Figure 1 is explicitly a cost/accuracy chart. The inter-assessor numbers I quoted from it are third-party (Scholer 2013, Cormack 1998, Castillo 2006) and I would trust those; the 'LLMs beat every human population' headline I would not, without an independent replication I did not have budget to find.
